source_refs.note: Topic 9.11 with Fig. 9.21 and the side boxes (PDF 209-210, printed 206-207). The drift-velocity example repeats the number 9.6 and its solution prints 2 x 10^4 for 2 x 10^-6; findings recorded.

blocks.text: Consider a segment of a current-carrying conductor of length L and area of cross-section A. The volume of the segment is AL (Fig. 9.21). Let n be the number of charge carriers per unit volume; then the total number of charge carriers in the segment at any time is nAL. If the charge on a carrier is q, the total charge present inside the segment at any instant is Q = nALq ... (9.29). Usually the charge carriers in a conductor are free electrons, which have negative charge.

blocks.alt: A segment of a conductor of length L and cross-section A filled with negative charge carriers drifting to the left with velocity v, so the current I flows to the right. A box gives I = n A v q for n carriers per cubic metre each of charge q.
blocks.caption: Negative charge carriers drifting in a conductor (original diagram after Figure 9.21).

blocks.text: Suppose the charge carriers move towards the left face of the segment when a potential difference is applied across the conductor; the electric current is then directed towards the right face. If the drift velocity of the carriers is v, the time taken by all the carriers originally present in the segment to exit through the left face is t = L/v. By the definition of current, I = Q/t. Putting in the values of Q and t, I = nALq/(L/v), or I = nAvq ... (9.30).

blocks.title: Example 9.6
blocks.text: A copper wire has a cross-sectional area of 2 x 10^-6 m^2 and carries a current of 3 A. If the number of electrons per unit volume is 8.5 x 10^28 m^-3, calculate the drift velocity of the electrons (e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C). Solution: I = Anvq, so 3 = (2 x 10^-6)(8.5 x 10^28) v (1.6 x 10^-19), giving v = 1.1 x 10^-4 m s^-1.
